title: Bram and the Borrowed Shortcut
markdown:
Once, in a morning still wearing mist like a downy blanket, Bram the hare longed to visit his friend Haf Badger, whose home lay beyond the Whispering Willows. Bram was quick as a flicker, the soft brown of warm earth. His whiskers twitched. He wanted to be there now, with the dawn only just yawning. He leaped from his cozy burrow, hunting the swiftest way.

At the edge of the Whispering Woods he met Celandine the unicorn. Her coat shimmered like pearly moonlight; her horn caught the first rays and scattered tiny rainbows. She was pausing to nibble a sweet cupcake from a curious tree that grew them, vanilla and ripe berries. Her eyes, a calm stream, watched him with quiet warmth.

“Good morning, Bram,” she chimed, silver bells on a breeze. “Where are you off to so quickly? The world is still waking.”

“To Haf’s,” Bram puffed. “I’m looking for the shortcut. Much faster.” He scanned for a path that promised speed.

Celandine smiled, slow. “A shortcut? Every true path wants noticing. The forest is not merely a place to hurry through. Do you see the moss on the north of that oak? The ladybugs on the ferns? Those are the forest’s quiet stories. They often lead you where you need to go.” She nudged a small blue-frosted cupcake toward him. “A taste. It may settle your thoughts.”

Bram declined, though wild strawberry tickled his nose. “Thank you. I haven’t time for lingering. I must get to Haf’s before the sun grows warm.” Then he spotted pale weathered bark by a slender birch, a crooked arrow into the dense woods. “A signpost. The shortcut. Wonderful luck.”

Celandine’s honey-coloured eyes followed. “Are you sure? That bark looks worn. Perhaps only a fallen branch. True paths unfold slowly. If it were a shortcut, would it hide in such shadow?”

But Bram was already a blur. “Thank you for the thought.” He plunged in, expecting a swift trail, a ribbon of easy earth. Instead the undergrowth thickened as if the woods had opinions. Dewy branches caught his fur and decorated him with leaves he had not asked to wear. Prickly brambles reached, tugged, made each bound a negotiation. He hopped left because left looked faster, then right because right looked clearer, and found himself in a stand of young hazel that all looked like the same mistake. A winding maze, a slow frustrating dance. A blackbird told him, without being asked, that he was going in circles, which was rude and accurate. No shortcut. The bark had been a trick of weather, or of haste, a crooked arrow that pointed only at wanting. A prickle of annoyance, then a whisper of worry. He thought of Haf’s chimney and could not smell it yet.

Meanwhile Celandine took the winding deer trail, unhurried. Small hooves on moss, like whispering leaves. She paused to watch mice waddle, counted seven ladybirds on a single fern, listened to a hidden brook’s lullaby, and enjoyed another wild strawberry cupcake as if sweetness were a kind of map. A fox crossed ahead, polite, unhurried too. She nodded. The fox, who had places to be and was not late, nodded back. Each step a quiet joy, a gentle discovery. The forest, noticed, made room.

After much pushing and pulling, after a ditch that was deeper than a hare’s optimism, Bram tumbled from the prickly bushes, blinking, decorated in burrs like a badly planned festival. Sunlight felt almost rude. He looked around, a bit dizzy, expecting more woods, and then his eyes widened. There ahead was Haf Badger’s cozy burrow, smoke curling from the chimney, the very chimney he had been smelling for in the brambles and never found. And sitting beside Haf, sipping sweet clover tea from a cup that had a chip and did not mind, was Celandine, serene as a long lovely nap, coat gleaming in dappled light, not a bramble on her.

Bram’s ears drooped. Fur ruffled. “Celandine,” he whispered, “I think I got a little lost. Harder than I thought. I’m very tired.”

She nodded, eyes kind, and did not make a speech of it. She poured him tea that smelled of clover and of not being late after all. Haf, who had been expecting a hare and had put out a third cup just in case, slid a plate of oat biscuits closer with a claw and pretended not to notice the burrs.

And so the hurried heart misses the sweetest miles, while the noticed path arrives with tea still warm.

The sun, a mellow glow, laid long lazy shadows on the meadow. Bram felt a gentle tiredness, pleasant in the limbs. He snuggled near Haf’s warm burrow, wonderfully safe. The woods, which had not been a shortcut, had been a teacher after all, and not a cruel one. Soon the soft world melted into dreams, and Celandine, humming like a kettle, watched the cupcake tree catch the last of the morning as if even sugar knew how to take its time.
characters: Bram (a hare), Celandine (a unicorn from a cupcake glade), Haf (a badger)
